newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Schuessel says EU and NATO inseparable.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Schuessel says EU and NATO inseparable.

text.p: Austrian Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel said on Sunday the enlargement of the European Union and of NATO were inextricably linked and that neutral Austria should join the Western military alliance.
"The EU and NATO are complementary expressions of the same community of values and solidarity," Schuessel told a forum on Europe in a monastery in the Wachau region outside Vienna.

He said security in Europe could only be assured by means of "a triangle of forces" between the EU, the Western European Union -- the defence arm of the EU -- and a new NATO with close ties to its former Cold War adversaries.
Austria should join all three on the grounds of its geographical position between the former east and west blocs, he said. Austria joined the EU in January 1995.
Schuessel said the planned eastward expansion of the EU and of NATO would contribute to stability in Europe and make the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe irreversible.
The new NATO was "the only fully functioning security and defence organisation in Europe", he said.
Moreover, the conflict in ex-Yugoslavia had showed that military strength and the presence of the United States were vital for any effective crisis management in Europe, he added.

Schuessel, leader of the conservative People's Party, has only recently backed Austrian membership of NATO unequivocally -- a move most of his dominant Social Democrat coalition partners adamantly oppose.
Recent opinion polls suggest a majority of Austrians, disillusioned with EU membership, would reject NATO entry.
Schuessel proposed a "Partnership for Europe" for the EU enlargement candidates, along the lines of NATO's Partnership for Peace military cooperation programme for countries in eastern Europe.
The candidates should be included in a flexible, multilateral framework tailored to their respective interests, he suggested. Norway and Switzerland should be included in such a partnership, he said.
During the Cold War, the Soviet Union, which occupied Austria after World War Two with fellow victors Britain, France and the United States, insisted that Austria must remain neutral.
It pulled its troops out of the country in 1955 only on condition that neutrality was enshrined in the constitution.
